---
title: "Sound 10: The Compressor"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

A **compressor** is an automatic hand on the volume knob. When the sound gets louder than a set level,
it turns it down; when it gets quieter, it lets it back up. The loud parts and the quiet parts end up
closer together. Almost every vocal, bass line and drum track on a record goes through one.

**How to use the page.** The source starts as an **uneven riff** (some notes loud, some barely
there). The graph shows input level across and output level up. The red dot is the sound right now,
and the red bar on the right is the **gain reduction**: how many decibels the compressor is turning the
sound down at this moment.

## The controls

<div class="sk" data-w="compressor" data-source="uneven"></div>

- **Threshold**: the level where the compressor starts working. Anything quieter passes through
  unchanged; on the graph the line follows the dashed diagonal until the threshold.
- **Ratio**: how hard it turns down what goes over. At 4 : 1, a sound 8 dB over the threshold comes out
  only 2 dB over. At 20 : 1 almost nothing gets over: that's a **limiter**.
- **Knee**: how gently it starts. A soft knee bends into compression gradually.
- **Attack**: how fast it reacts when the sound goes over. Slow attack lets the very start of each
  note through before clamping down, which keeps drums punchy.
- **Release**: how fast it lets go when the sound drops back.
- **Make-up gain**: compression makes everything quieter, so you turn the whole thing back up. Now
  the quiet notes are louder than before.

Press **Bypass** on and off with the uneven riff: compressed, the quiet notes come forward and the
loud ones stop jumping out.

## Hearing attack and release

Switch the source to the **drum loop**, set the ratio to 8 : 1 and the threshold to about −30 dB.

- **Attack 1 ms**: the snare's crack is flattened; the drums sound small and thick.
- **Attack 30 ms**: the crack gets through before the compressor reacts; the drums *punch*.
- **Release 30 ms** with a fast attack: the sound "pumps", rising between hits. Dance music uses
  this on purpose.

## Parallel compression

Turn **Mix** down to 50%. Now you hear the untouched drums *and* a heavily squashed copy together.
The natural hits stay sharp and the squashed copy fills in between them. Engineers call it
"New York" compression.

## Your own playing

Choose **Microphone** (headphones on) and play or sing from very soft to loud. With a threshold of
−40 dB and a ratio of 6 : 1, watch the gain reduction bar follow you. The site's backing band runs
through a compressor too (threshold −12 dB, ratio 4 : 1, attack 3 ms), and these sound pages end in a
limiter so that nothing comes out too loud.
